verses.text: After many days, Yahweh’s word came to Elijah, in the third year, saying, “Go, show yourself to Ahab; and I will send rain on the earth.”
Elijah went to show himself to Ahab. The famine was severe in Samaria.
Ahab called Obadiah, who was over the household. (Now Obadiah feared Yahweh greatly;
for when Jezebel cut off Yahweh’s prophets, Obadiah took one hundred prophets, and hid them by fifty in a cave, and fed them with bread and water.)
Ahab said to Obadiah, “Go through the land, to all the springs of water, and to all the brooks. Perhaps we may find grass and save the horses and mules alive, that we not lose all the animals.”
So they divided the land between them to pass throughout it. Ahab went one way by himself, and Obadiah went another way by himself.
As Obadiah was on the way, behold, Elijah met him. He recognized him, and fell on his face, and said, “Is it you, my lord Elijah?”
He answered him, “It is I. Go, tell your lord, ‘Behold, Elijah is here!’”
He said, “How have I sinned, that you would deliver your servant into the hand of Ahab, to kill me?
As Yahweh your God lives, there is no nation or kingdom where my lord has not sent to seek you. When they said, ‘He is not here,’ he took an oath of the kingdom and nation, that they didn’t find you.
Now you say, ‘Go, tell your lord, “Behold, Elijah is here.”’

It will happen, as soon as I leave you, that Yahweh’s Spirit will carry you I don’t know where; and so when I come and tell Ahab, and he can’t find you, he will kill me. But I, your servant, have feared Yahweh from my youth.
Wasn’t it told my lord what I did when Jezebel killed Yahweh’s prophets, how I hid one hundred men of Yahweh’s prophets with fifty to a cave, and fed them with bread and water?
Now you say, ‘Go, tell your lord, “Behold, Elijah is here”.’ He will kill me.”
Elijah said, “As Yahweh of Armies lives, before whom I stand, I will surely show myself to him today.”
So Obadiah went to meet Ahab, and told him; and Ahab went to meet Elijah.
When Ahab saw Elijah, Ahab said to him, “Is that you, you troubler of Israel?”
He answered, “I have not troubled Israel; but you, and your father’s house, in that you have forsaken Yahweh’s commandments, and you have followed the Baals.
Now therefore send, and gather to me all Israel to Mount Carmel, and four hundred fifty of the prophets of Baal, and four hundred of the prophets of the Asherah, who eat at Jezebel’s table.”
So Ahab sent to all the children of Israel, and gathered the prophets together to Mount Carmel.
Elijah came near to all the people, and said, “How long will you waver between the two sides? If Yahweh is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him.” The people didn’t say a word.
Then Elijah said to the people, “I, even I only, am left as a prophet of Yahweh; but Baal’s prophets are four hundred fifty men.

Let them therefore give us two bulls; and let them choose one bull for themselves, and cut it in pieces, and lay it on the wood, and put no fire under; and I will dress the other bull, and lay it on the wood, and put no fire under it.
You call on the name of your god, and I will call on Yahweh’s name. The God who answers by fire, let him be God.” All the people answered, “What you say is good.”
Elijah said to the prophets of Baal, “Choose one bull for yourselves, and dress it first; for you are many; and call on the name of your god, but put no fire under it.”

They took the bull which was given them, and they dressed it, and called on the name of Baal from morning even until noon, saying, “Baal, hear us!” But there was no voice, and nobody answered. They leaped about the altar which was made.
At noon, Elijah mocked them, and said, “Cry aloud; for he is a god. Either he is deep in thought, or he has gone somewhere, or he is on a journey, or perhaps he sleeps and must be awakened.”
They cried aloud, and cut themselves in their way with knives and lances, until the blood gushed out on them.
When midday was past, they prophesied until the time of the evening offering; but there was no voice, no answer, and nobody paid attention.
Elijah said to all the people, “Come near to me!”; and all the people came near to him. He repaired Yahweh’s altar that had been thrown down.
Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom Yahweh’s word came, saying, “Israel shall be your name.”
With the stones he built an altar in Yahweh’s name. He made a trench around the altar, large enough to contain two seahs  of seed.
He put the wood in order, and cut the bull in pieces, and laid it on the wood. He said, “Fill four jars with water, and pour it on the burnt offering, and on the wood.”
He said, “Do it a second time”; and they did it the second time. He said, “Do it a third time”; and they did it the third time.
The water ran around the altar; and he also filled the trench with water.

At the time of the evening offering, Elijah the prophet came near, and said, “Yahweh, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Israel, let it be known today that you are God in Israel, and that I am your servant, and that I have done all these things at your word.
Hear me, Yahweh, hear me, that this people may know that you, Yahweh, are God, and that you have turned their heart back again.”
Then Yahweh’s fire fell, and consumed the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench.
When all the people saw it, they fell on their faces. They said, “Yahweh, he is God! Yahweh, he is God!”
Elijah said to them, “Seize the prophets of Baal! Don’t let one of them escape!” They seized them; and Elijah brought them down to the brook Kishon, and killed them there.
Elijah said to Ahab, “Get up, eat and drink; for there is the sound of abundance of rain.”
So Ahab went up to eat and to drink. Elijah went up to the top of Carmel; and he bowed himself down on the earth, and put his face between his knees.
He said to his servant, “Go up now, and look toward the sea.” He went up, and looked, and said, “There is nothing.” He said, “Go again” seven times.
On the seventh time, he said, “Behold, a small cloud, like a man’s hand, is rising out of the sea.” He said, “Go up, tell Ahab, ‘Get ready and go down, so that the rain doesn’t stop you.’”
In a little while, the sky grew black with clouds and wind, and there was a great rain. Ahab rode, and went to Jezreel.
Yahweh’s hand was on Elijah; and he tucked his cloak into his belt and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.

footnotes.content: After three long years of drought, the word comes again—not as a whisper but a sending, a fresh calling into the front lines. Even in silence, God's clock was running; He knows exactly when the soil needs rain and when His people need to see His power plainly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Samaria was dying of thirst—animals, crops, hope itself seemed dried up. Into that bleakness Elijah walks, lean and faithful, like a lamp carried into a tomb. The famine was the stage; now came the God who feeds the ravens.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Obadiah—his very name means 'servant of Yahweh'—held a position of power in a wicked court, yet remained faithful. How many godly folk work in broken places, hidden, quietly honoring the Lord when no one in the halls around them knows?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: While Jezebel was butchering prophets, Obadiah was hiding them by fifties in caves, keeping them alive with bread and water. Faithful courage is often quiet—not marching or shouting, but steady mercy in the face of evil. That, too, is obedience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahab's desperation shows the depth of his blindness: he searches for grass to save horses while refusing the God who holds rain and seed in His hand. How often do we scramble to fix what only honest repentance can mend?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They split the land between them, two men searching the dried brooks. Neither knew that on one of those roads, the prophet was waiting—the very word made flesh that would change everything in one day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Obadiah's face-down fall was not fear but worship—he recognized the anointed of God standing before him. In that moment, his years of hidden faithfulness met the prophet his heart had served.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three words from Elijah: "It is I." After years of hiding, hunted, the prophet steps into the light. There is a moment for every faithful soul when concealment ends and the Lord says, 'Now is the time to stand.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Obadiah's fear is not cowardice but the weight of a conscience that trembles before God. He loves Yahweh; he's terrified of Ahab. And now Elijah asks him to walk into the trap that might be death.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every kingdom, every nation—Ahab's dragnet was vast, yet caught nothing. The Lord hides His prophets not just in caves but in the palm of His hand, beyond every hunter's reach. No king can snare what God holds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Obadiah repeats the command like a prayer, half disbelief. 'Go tell my lord.' These words are the doorway between the world he knows and the miracle he's about to witness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Obadiah's fear is real: the Spirit moves mysteriously, Elijah vanishes, Ahab kills him in rage. Yet he anchors his plea to the one unshakeable fact—'I, your servant, have feared Yahweh from my youth.' That fear is his strength, not his weakness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Obadiah lays out his faithfulness—one hundred prophets hidden, fed in secret—it's not boasting but a plea: 'Look, I have honored Yahweh even when the kingdom turned its back. Surely you know I'm not a traitor?'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three times he says the same word—'He will kill me.' Obadiah is speaking his deepest terror aloud, laying it before Elijah like a child placing a burden at a parent's feet: 'I'm afraid. Is this really what you're asking?'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elijah's oath—'As Yahweh of Armies lives, before whom I stand'—settles it. The prophet doesn't promise Obadiah safety; he promises certainty: I will show myself today. Sometimes faith means trusting not outcomes but the God who stands behind them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Obadiah goes. He carries the message up through the dusty road to his king, knowing each step might lead to his death, yet trusting the prophet's oath. That's obedience—not blindness, but faith despite the fear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahab's first word to Elijah: 'Troubler of Israel.' The king has it backward, as the wicked often do—he calls the healer a wound, the light a fire. But Elijah doesn't shrink from the name; he answers it straight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elijah flips the charge: 'You troubled Israel—you and your father's house, because you forsook the commandments and followed Baal.' Truth doesn't argue; it simply names what is. The drought wasn't sent by the prophet; it came because the throne chose idols over the God of rain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elijah gathers them to Mount Carmel—a place-name the story will make sacred. There, one prophet against 850 false ones: 450 of Baal, 400 of the Asherah, all fed at Jezebel's table. The numbers say the kingdom has chosen; now the kingdom will see who speaks truly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahab's command runs through the land like a fast-spreading shadow. Every false prophet gathers, and the people come to watch. The stage is set, though only one Man knows the ending.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'How long will you waver between two sides?' Elijah's question cuts through the crowd's silence like a sword. He's not scolding them for their faith—he's grieving their refusal to choose. Faithlessness hates the clarity of this choice; it prefers the blur of maybe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One man. Four hundred and fifty arrayed against him. By every count that the world keeps, Elijah is alone and lost. But he speaks as if he stands with armies, because he does—the armies of Yahweh stand with the one who names His name.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two bulls, two altars, no fire beneath either. A simple test: let the god answer by fire. The terms are humble, almost gentle—as if Elijah is saying, 'Let's see.' But behind the simple words is a stone certainty that only one fire will fall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people agree: 'What you say is good.' For one moment, even in their confusion, they assent to the test. The god who answers by fire—let him be God. They don't know they're about to see an answer so fierce and bright that wavering will end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elijah's courtesy is his confidence: 'You choose first; you are many.' He yields the ground of the test without yielding an inch of faith. Let them burn their prayers and cut themselves raw—it changes nothing about what comes next.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From morning to noon they cry: 'Baal, hear us!' But the altar is silent. Four hundred and fifty voices, beating themselves red, reaching toward a god who cannot hear because he is not. Emptiness cannot answer emptiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At noon, when the sun is highest and hope ought to stir, Elijah laughs. 'Cry aloud—perhaps he's lost in thought, or on a journey, or sleeping?' The mockery is kind, even—it's the laughter of a man watching children play with a broken toy, inviting them to look and see the truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They cut themselves until blood pours down. Desperation can drive a human soul to wound its own flesh, hoping the god will notice blood if not prayer. But self-harm is never the language the true God speaks or requires.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Past midday until evening—hours pass with no voice, no answer, no one paying attention. The prophets of Baal have given everything they have to give. The silence is now absolute. And in that silence, the true answer is about to come.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elijah gathers the exhausted crowd near, then begins to repair Yahweh's altar that had been thrown down. An act of restoration, done slowly, deliberately, with every eye watching. He's mending not just stones but the breach between heaven and a people meant to worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twelve stones, one for each tribe of Jacob—of all Israel, not just the northern kingdom divided now. Elijah is saying with his hands: 'This altar is for all God's people, whole, one, as He intended us to be.' The very stones speak of covenant and unity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He digs a trench around the altar, large enough to hold two seahs of seed. Every detail seems odd, almost wasteful—until you see what he's about to do. The trench will matter. Nothing Elijah does is careless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He arranges the wood, cuts the bull into pieces, lays it all bare for the people to see. Then: 'Fill four jars with water.' In a drought. Pouring water on an altar meant for fire. The people watch, maybe thinking him mad—until they begin to understand he's not afraid of how things look.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Second time. Third time. Twelve jars of water in all. The altar is drenched, the wood soaked, the trench running with water. Anyone could strike a match and fail; the water makes failure impossible. Elijah wants no room for doubt, no explanation except God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The water runs and runs, filling the trench, saturating the ground. A visual prayer: 'Lord, I am making it impossible for anyone to say I cheated, that I hid fire somewhere. Let the whole world see Your hand and know that You alone are God.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At the time of the evening offering, Elijah prays simply: 'Let it be known that You are God in Israel, that I am Your servant, and that I have done all this at Your word.' No flourish, no bargaining—just a clear request that echoes through heaven like a bell.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Hear me, Yahweh, that this people may know that You are God and that You have turned their heart back again.' Elijah prays not for himself but for the people—that they might come home, might turn, might belong to the God who loves them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then fire falls. It consumes the offering, the wood, the stones, the dust—and licks up the water in the trench. A fire so hot, so alive, so unmistakably God that no soul present could mistake its meaning. Heaven itself came down to answer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people fall on their faces. Their wavering ends. In that moment, they see with clarity what they'd been choosing to ignore: 'Yahweh, He is God! Yahweh, He is God!' The truth, spoken twice, as if saying it once was not enough after so much blindness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elijah commands: 'Seize the prophets of Baal; let not one escape.' What happened next at the brook Kishon is hard; it is the judgment of God rendered through a people who have finally seen. Mercy often has a sharp edge when it follows willful darkness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Elijah turns to the king: 'Get up, eat and drink; for there is the sound of abundance of rain.' Ahab hears the storm coming in the distance, the very thing the prophet promised three years ago. Judgment and mercy arrive together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: While Ahab eats, Elijah climbs Mount Carmel, bows to the earth, face between his knees. The fire is done; now comes prayer—the prayer of intercession, of labor, of a prophet standing in the gap between God's promise and the world that needs to see it fulfilled.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His servant looks toward the sea seven times. Six times: nothing. Elijah prays between each look, bending low, wrestling with heaven. Faith is not passive hoping—it is active, persistent, refusing to let go until the promise appears.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The seventh time: a cloud the size of a man's hand rises from the sea. Small. Almost nothing. Yet Elijah sees it and speaks with certainty: 'The rains are coming; tell Ahab to prepare.' He reads the smallest sign as if reading the face of God Himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sky darkens, the wind rises, the great rain falls. Three years of drought end in a single afternoon. The earth drinks again; the people drink again; the land tastes mercy. Ahab rides toward Jezreel, but he cannot outrun what has changed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this image: Yahweh's hand is on Elijah; he tucks his cloak and runs before the king. The prophet who'd hidden in caves now runs in the open, empowered by the very God who'd called him through the drought. As of 2026-10, we know that same hand still reaches for those whom He calls to faithfulness—not always to comfort, but always to purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
